Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 representative generative models with thorough ablation studies

Strong and consistent practical improvements across both autoregressive and non-autoregressive models (e.g., MAR-B FID 2.31→1.55, RandomAR 11.78→5.22)

Unexplained model-specific behavior: additive noise improves MAR but not SiT; paper speculates but doesn't investigate, suggesting incomplete understanding of mechanisms

Limited conceptual novelty: denoising autoencoders (2008) and masked autoencoders (2022) are established; interpolative vs. additive noise is minor technical contribution; core value is empirical validation
Hyperparameter complexity not addressed: introduces γ (noise std.), M (masking ratio), and biased uniform distribution for masking (Eq. 5) with no principled guidance for new settings
Incomplete analysis: no visualization of learned latent spaces, no investigation of what structural changes occur in representations, limited analysis of why interpolative noise works better
No statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; single runs reported (though evaluated on 50k samples)
Modest improvements for some models: SiT shows ~26% relative improvement; DiT/LightningDiT don't dramatically exceed semantics-distilled methods, limiting broader impact

Comparison fairness concerns: semantics-distilled baselines use external encoders (different resources); proposed method applies both noise and masking (extra supervised signal vs. no denoising in baselines)

strengths: Clear and intuitive motivation: unified view of modern generative models as performing denoising is elegant and well-articulated
Strong empirical results: particularly impressive improvements on AR models (MAR 3.71→2.43 FID, RandomAR 11.78→5.22 FID)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: thorough ablations, tests across 6 diverse models (3 AR, 3 non-AR)
Valuable empirical finding: reveals that semantics-distilled tokenizers fail on AR models despite working on non-AR models
Good generalization: works well across both paradigms without external pretrained encoders, unlike VA-VAE and MAETok
Detailed reproducibility information: extensive appendix with hyperparameters, computational costs, and pseudocode
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is relatively straightforward—training a denoising autoencoder in latent space using interpolative noise and masking, both known techniques

Unresolved training-inference discrepancy: decoder trained on corrupted latents but operates on clean latents; proposed fine-tuning solution is ad-hoc and undermines the stated motivation that 'robust latents' matter
Shallow explanation of why method works: lacks analysis of what properties l-DeTok latents possess; why corrupted latent training helps is not explained beyond circular reasoning
Insufficient representation analysis: no visualization or characterization of learned latent spaces compared to standard VAE; no analysis of disentanglement, smoothness, or robustness properties
Limited evaluation scope: only ImageNet 256×256; no evaluation on other datasets or resolutions, making generalization claims overstated

Questionable comparison fairness: semantics-distilled baselines may not be optimally tuned; authors modified generative model implementations (CFG on all channels); unclear if poor baseline performance is fundamental or tuning

Inconsistent results across models: different models respond differently to design choices (additive noise helps MAR but not SiT; masking provides minimal benefit for SiT); suggests method may be less general than claimed
Hyperparameter choices lack justification: γ=3.0 and M=0.7 appear somewhat arbitrary; limited sensitivity analysis on why these specific values
Decoder fine-tuning inflates results: Table 3 improvements from fine-tuning (1.61→1.55 for MAR-B) are non-trivial; unclear how much comes from latent denoising vs. fine-tuning
Missing baselines: no comparison to other recent tokenizer methods (FlexTok, Diffusion autoencoders) mentioned in references
No computational cost analysis: 1,150 A100 GPU hours for B-B tokenizer training; unclear if cost is justified or if similar gains achievable with less training

Limited novelty of core idea: connection between VAE reconstruction and denoising is well-known; masked autoencoders already use corruption-based training; the insight about downstream alignment is valuable but not deeply novel

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight: aligning tokenizer training with the unified denoising objective shared by modern generative models is elegant and compelling
Comprehensive experimental validation across 6 representative models (3 non-AR, 3 AR) with thorough ablations on noise design, masking strategies, and combinations
Significant empirical improvements: ~34% FID reduction for MAR-B (3.71→2.43), ~56% for RandomAR, and MAR-B achieves FID 1.55 matching original MAR-H

Important methodological discovery: reveals that semantics-distilled tokenizers severely degrade autoregressive models despite improving diffusion models, challenging prior assumptions about tokenizer generalization
Practical and accessible method that avoids dependencies on large-scale pretrained vision encoders, unlike distillation-based approaches
Strong reproducibility: detailed architecture specifications, hyperparameter documentation, training procedures, computational costs, and promised code release

Insightful ablations with clear findings: interpolative noise superiority, optimal masking ratios (70-90%), benefits of randomized over constant masking, and interplay between latent noise and masking
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: only ImageNet 256×256; no evaluation at higher resolutions (512×512, 1024×1024) or other datasets, undermining claims about generalizability and practical applicability

Training-inference discrepancy is inelegant and conceptually concerning: decoder trained on noise-corrupted latents but operates on clean embeddings at inference, requiring additional 100-epoch fine-tuning to recover performance
Limited tokenizer scope: only continuous tokenizers explored; discrete/VQ tokenizers completely absent despite being widely used in practice

Insufficient theoretical understanding: lacks formal analysis of why this objective helps both AR and non-AR models despite their different denoising mechanisms; model-specific behaviors (additive noise helps MAR but not SiT) are unexplained
Computational cost not analyzed: B-B tokenizer requires ~1,150 A100 hours for training, but no comparison against baseline or semantics-distilled alternatives; cost-benefit analysis missing

Experimental design concerns: baseline tokenizer comparability unclear, different training epochs across experiments (100 vs. 800), potential fairness issues when comparing against publicly available tokenizers

Overstated generalization claims: 'broad generalizability' and 'universal tokenizer' claims tested only on 6 ImageNet-trained models at one resolution; cross-dataset transfer and higher-resolution scalability unexplored
Presentation issues: Figures 2 and 3 have overlapping lines making comparisons difficult; notation inconsistencies; missing analysis of when/why the approach fails or has boundary conditions

strengths: Clear conceptual motivation: elegant unification of diffusion and autoregressive models under 'denoising' perspective provides good intuition for design choices

Comprehensive experimental validation: evaluates across 6 generative models (3 non-AR, 3 AR), multiple datasets (ImageNet 256/512×256, MS-COCO), and diverse tokenizer types (2D/1D continuous, VQ, CNN/ViT), which is more extensive than typical tokenizer papers

Strong empirical results: consistent FID improvements across all generative model types, particularly for AR models (34-56% gains), achieving state-of-the-art on MAR without requiring external pretrained teachers
Important discovery: reveals that tokenizer improvements don't transfer between AR and non-AR paradigms, challenging prior assumptions and providing valuable design insights
Thorough ablations and analysis: systematic study of noise properties, masking ratios, and joint denoising with clear justification for design choices (interpolative vs additive noise)
Reproducibility: detailed implementation details, pseudo-code, standardized training procedures, and extensive appendix enable reproduction
No computational overhead: Table A.2 demonstrates training time nearly identical to baseline tokenizers, making it practical to deploy
Scalability analysis: Table 3 shows consistent improvements across model sizes (S/B/L for both SiT and MAR)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: denoising autoencoders are well-established; connection between tokenizer-level corruption and downstream generative performance is assumed rather than rigorously justified

Lack of theoretical understanding: no principled analysis of why this approach works, why γ=3.0 is optimal, or how corruption resistance maps to downstream task performance (acknowledged in Appendix D)

Training-inference discrepancy: decoder trained on corrupted latents operates on clean latents at inference; workaround of 10-epoch decoder fine-tuning (improving MAR-L FID 1.43→1.35) suggests the issue is non-trivial and deserves deeper investigation rather than a patch

Robustness concerns: Section A.6 reveals delayed 'grokking' when applying l-DeTok to 1D tokenizers, requiring ad-hoc warm-up schedule; raises questions about generalizability across architectures despite claims of being architecture-agnostic

Incomplete analysis of design choices: limited explanation for why masking benefits AR more than non-AR, why interpolative noise is 'critical' (difference from additive noise is practical rather than fundamental), or what principles govern optimal corruption levels

Mixed results on non-AR models: Table 4 shows distilled baselines (VA-VAE, MAETok) achieve comparable FID on non-AR models; advantage over these approaches is primarily avoiding external teachers rather than superior performance
Scaling limitations: experiments at moderate scale (O(10⁶) samples); unclear how method scales to web-scale models and datasets; authors acknowledge this as future work

Evaluation limitations: relies primarily on FID/IS with known limitations; text-to-image improvements ('spot artifacts') mentioned qualitatively but not quantified; no human evaluation or error bars across runs

Critical details relegated to appendix: necessity and implications of decoder fine-tuning, 1D tokenizer grokking issues, and Section A.3's interesting finding that decoder-only fine-tuning hurts performance deserve main paper discussion

Unfixed hyperparameters: standard training recipe not tuned per-tokenizer-generative-model combination; loss weights (Eq. 6) use defaults without sensitivity analysis; noise schedule exploration limited despite Table 1 suggesting sensitivity

strengths: Clear and intuitive motivation: The observation that generative models share a common denoising objective naturally motivates training tokenizers to produce robust embeddings.

Exceptional experimental comprehensiveness: Tests across 6 generative models, multiple datasets/resolutions, thorough ablations, and extensions to 1D/VQ/CNN architectures. Reproducibility is exemplary with detailed hyperparameters and pseudo-code.
Strong empirical results without external supervision: Achieves MAR-B FID of 1.55 (from 2.31) without semantics distillation, making it practical for domains lacking pretrained models.
Consistent generalization: Improvements persist across AR/non-AR models and architectural choices, suggesting a robust principle.
Honest methodology: Appendix transparently discusses training challenges, trade-offs, and discrepancies, aiding reproducibility and trust.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core contribution is straightforward (corrupt latents during training, reconstruct)—relatively minor technical advance. Interpolative vs. additive noise is justified empirically but not rigorously. Masking is borrowed directly from MAE without new insights.

Lacking theoretical understanding: Paper doesn't explain why this objective produces better embeddings or what properties are being optimized. Authors acknowledge limited understanding (Appendix D). No analysis of embedding space structure or divergence from baselines.

Training-inference discrepancy undermines claims: Decoder trained on noise-corrupted latents but operates on clean embeddings at inference. Addressed via 10-epoch fine-tuning (a patch solution). Notably, fine-tuning only the decoder while freezing the encoder worsens performance, suggesting gains come from the encoder, but the mechanism is opaque.

Insufficient isolation of contributing factors: Multiple ablations show improvements but don't reveal which is most critical. Masking adds little for SiT-B; for non-AR models, gains are modest. No analysis of which model types benefit most or why.

Methodological gaps: No error bars/confidence intervals; single runs for most experiments. Hyperparameters (masking bias, γ = 3.0, warm-up schedules) appear ad-hoc. 'Grokking' phenomenon in 1D tokenizers suggests optimization fragility. Different CFG scales per method could introduce bias.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated insight unifying denoising across generative model paradigms
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 diverse generative models with extensive ablations
Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art for MAR models without semantics distillation (FID 1.35 for MAR-L)
Excellent generalization: works across AR/non-AR models, multiple architectures (ViT/CNN), and tokenizer topologies (2D/1D/VQ)
Important practical finding that semantics-distilled tokenizers fail to generalize to AR models while l-DeTok does
Independence from external pretrained models makes it applicable to domains like video and audio
Thorough reproducibility with extensive implementation details, promised code, and training cost analysis
Addresses practical issues (grokking phenomenon in 1D tokenizers) with concrete solutions
weaknesses: Limited theoretical understanding of why denoising helps; core design choices (interpolative noise, noise schedules) lack principled justification

Training-inference discrepancy: decoder trained on corrupted latents but operates on clean embeddings; requires 100-epoch fine-tuning to recover performance, suggesting gains may primarily come from encoder regularization rather than the denoising objective itself
Moderate experimental scale (O(10^6) samples) with no evidence of scaling to web-scale; acknowledged as open question
Limited technical novelty: applies well-established denoising autoencoders and masking (MAE) to tokenizers; incremental contribution
Incomplete analysis: latent noise alone nearly achieves joint results for non-AR models (5.56 vs 5.50 FID), yet masking is included without clear justification
No error bars or variance estimates; CFG scale selection 'searched from FID@10k' could overfit to this metric
Multiple design choices appear ad-hoc: masking ratio bias (Eq. 5), GAN loss timing at epoch 100, noise schedule variations showing similar results
Mechanism of spot artifact removal in text-to-image generation unexplained
